newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols mixed ahead of weekend.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols mixed ahead of weekend.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. fixed-income options ended narrowly mixed, sandwiched between fears stemming from weak bond prices and weekend time-decay pressure, dealers said.
They said the stock market's sharp reversal to the downside late on Thursday had stirred nervousness in the bond market, depressing bond prices and supporting volatilities.
"It (implied volatility) went a little higher this morning, I think because the stock market dropped yesterday after we closed," a brokerage firm trader at the Chicago Board of Trade said.
"We really didn't have any economic data to speak of today, so I guess we were just watching the stock market," he added.
Implied volatility for CBOT March T-bond futures options stood at about 10.5 percent just before the close, marginally off early highs and virtually unchanged from Thursday.

One of the largest trades in the CBOT pit today was a 10,000-contract March/June 112 call spread by a U.S. bank. Traders said the deal was apparently a rollover of an existing position rather than a totally fresh position, given its size.

February T-bond futures options expired today. Traders said the expiration of the serial options caused no noticeable distortion to the underlying market and there were no large trades in February contracts.
Implied volatilities for the shorter end of the yield curve were slightly softer, particularly for the shorter-dated options.

Implied volatility for June Eurodollar futures options on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange was off a quarter point to about 11.9 percent, while September was off 0.1 to around 14.9 and December steady at about 16.4 percent.

Traders said the shorter-dated Eurodollar options, besides having higher time-decay rates than their longer-dated counterparts, were stymied by a stagnation of their underlying futures contracts. Front-month Eurodollar futures tend to gravitate toward levels at parity with cash deposits.
"People seem to be comfortable with the idea that there's not going to be a rate hike soon, although there could be something later in the year," a brokerage trader at CME said.
June 94.00 puts, which have had volume throughout the week, continued to see good demand. One firm was said to have bought 2,000 contracts.

A Swiss bank affiliate was said to have traded 7,000 contracts in the front-February 94.25/94.50 squash -- buying the 94.25 puts and selling the 94.50 calls -- paying slightly more for the puts than it received for the calls.

Traders said the market's focus next week would initially be on Tuesday's fourth-quarter U.S. employment cost index amid concerns that a tight labor market could eventually fuel inflation. Economists polled by Reuters have, on average, forecast an increase of around one percent against a gain of 0.6 percent in the previus quarter.
